title.analysis: Authentic title "Stop Thinking Poor: The Mindset of the 1%" is an imperative plus an elite-identity frame ("the 1%"). The script delivers 11 "mental shifts" contrasting "poor" and "wealthy" thinking; it never defines the 1% or gives a wealth or income threshold. TYPICAL against the cohort. Association only.

They didn't inherit secret family fortunes, and they're definitely not using some mystical money manifestation technique they learned from a guru on Instagram. Yet, somehow they're building wealth while you're wondering where your paycheck disappeared to. Again, here's what's really happening. The top 1% don't just
script.ending_words: along, maybe even take some notes, and then go right back to thinking exactly the same way you did before clicking on this video. That's not me being pessimistic. That's just human nature. Um, but for those of you who actually implement even half of these concepts, your financial future just changed dramatically. The choice is yours. And frankly, your bank account will reflect whatever you decide to do next.
script.analysis: Full 20425 canonical characters read. A list essay of 11 mindset "shifts": hook (others glide through life); assets vs liabilities; decades-long time horizon (tax refund as loan); financial education and 80/20 behaviour; creating vs consuming; risk (savings 0.5% vs 3% inflation; 10% market average); taxes ($200K at 40% vs $150K at 20%); leverage; generosity and abundance; information and action; money velocity ($5,000 example); strategic impatience; challenge close. Few numbers. Directly verified: CPI inflation ~3% at upload (FRED). Wrong: the tax example leaves both earners with exactly $120,000, so "keeping less" is false. Unsupported: "80% behaviour". Moralising "poor people" framing; much repetition. The stored ending is complete.

claim_audit.assessment: [INDEPENDENT_CALCULATION_VERIFIED] $200,000 x 0.60 = $120,000 and $150,000 x 0.80 = $120,000: both keep exactly the same amount, so "keeping less" is false as stated. [ANALYST_RECALL_NOT_REVERIFIED] A 40% all-in effective rate on $200,000 is far above typical US combined federal income plus payroll effective rates (roughly 20-30%), so the example is also unrealistic.
